meta.title: Seven Countries Claim the Same Slice of Antarctica
meta._convention: One scene-spec JSON per script, saved alongside it as <script-name>.scenes.json. Each beat's `duration` is intentionally omitted here -- build_video.js fills it in at render time from the ACTUAL measured length of that beat's generated narration WAV.
meta._note_antarctica: Antarctica (numeric id 010, alpha-2 AQ added to maps/country-codes.json) IS present as a landmass polygon in world-atlas's 110m countries topology (confirmed empirically), so it uses the standard `highlight` convention for the continent itself. The three overlapping national claims (UK/Chile/Argentina) are NOT separate polygons in the dataset -- those are hand-drawn dashed 'wedge' `lines` (two rays from an interior apex point down to two coastal longitudes, per real claim boundaries: UK 20W-80W, Chile 53W-90W, Argentina 25W-74W), following the 'scenes that aren't a country' line-drawing convention layered on top of the real Antarctica landmass. Camera boxes deliberately stay north of -80 latitude to avoid Mercator's polar scale blowup near -90.

beats.voText: No one owns Antarctica. But seven countries have officially claimed slices of it anyway, and some of those slices overlap completely.
Each claim is a wedge running from the coast toward the South Pole, like a slice of pie, one country's slice per claim, in theory.
beats.onScreenText: Slices of pie, pointing at the Pole.

beats.voText: The UK, Chile, and Argentina all claim the exact same wedge: the Antarctic Peninsula, the part of the continent closest to South America.
Their claims overlap by tens of thousands of square miles, the same ground claimed three separate times, by three separate governments.
The 1959 Antarctic Treaty froze every claim in place, no new ones, no enforcing old ones, making this the largest land on Earth with no real owner.
Seven claims, three of them stacked on the same wedge, and a treaty that just leaves it all in limbo. Follow for more places on Earth that shouldn't exist, but do.
